Poseidon. The Olympian god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses in Greek mythology, ruling from his underwater palace with his trident-bearing authority. One of the twelve Olympians and brother to Zeus and Hades, Poseidon appears throughout Greek epic and drama as a volatile, passionate, vengeful deity whose wrath shipwrecks heroes and whose favor grants safe passage. He embodies the sea's dual nature: life-giving and catastrophic, fertile and destructive.

Poseidon is one of the three paramount gods alongside Zeus and Hades, each ruling a cosmic domain. Zeus governs the sky, Hades the underworld, and Poseidon the sea, a tripartite sovereignty of the universe. Armed with a trident, which he uses to shake the earth, cause earthquakes, and churn the sea, the trident is his symbol of power and appears in art as his defining attribute. He rules the ocean realm from a golden palace in the sea depths. He controls storms, currents, tides, and the fate of sailors. Sailors prayed to him before voyages and made offerings for safe passage.

He is the father of Medusa in some versions and thus linked to her monstrous transformation. He also fathered numerous sea-nymphs called Nereids and monsters like Polyphemus the Cyclops. He harbors implacable enmity toward Odysseus in The Odyssey, repeatedly delaying his homecoming and destroying ships. His decade-long vendetta against Odysseus is the epic's central antagonistic force. He competed with Athena for patronage of Athens. She won by offering the olive tree, while Poseidon's gift of a salt-water spring was deemed less valuable, a myth explaining Athena's pre-eminence in the city.

He is linked to horses through origin myths. Some accounts claim he created horses by striking the earth with his trident. He appears as a horse-god in pre-Olympian cults, suggesting an older fertility deity absorbed into the Olympian pantheon. His brother Zeus ranks above him in authority, and unlike the austere Hades, Poseidon is volatile and vengeful, embodying the sea's unpredictable and often destructive power.
